content: 1. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) was tasked with providing a scientific opinion on trans fats within the European Union. 2. In October 2005, the United Kingdom's Food Standards Agency (FSA) advocated for improved labeling of trans fats in food products. 3. An editorial in the July 29, 2006, issue of the British Medical Journal also called for better labeling of trans fats. 4. In January 2007, the British Retail Consortium announced that major UK retailers, including ASDA, Boots, Co-op, Iceland, Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury's, Tesco, and Waitrose, planned to eliminate trans fatty acids from their own-brand products by the end of 2007. 5. Sainsbury's became the first major UK retailer to completely remove trans fats from all their own-brand food products. 6. On December 13, 2007, the Food Standards Agency issued a statement indicating that voluntary measures to reduce trans fats in food had already resulted in safe levels of consumer intake in the UK. 7. Prior to 2006, consumers in the United States could not directly determine the presence or quantity of trans fats in food products, as this information was only inferable from ingredient lists, particularly those containing partially hydrogenated oils. 8. On July 11, 2003, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a regulation requiring manufacturers to list trans fat content on the Nutrition Facts panel of food products and certain dietary supplements. 9. The new labeling rule allowed for immediate voluntary compliance, with mandatory compliance required by January 1, 2006, unless companies petitioned for an extension until January 1, 2008. 10. The FDA permitted foods containing less than 0.5 grams of trans fat per serving to be labeled as containing 0 grams of trans fat. 11. The FDA did not approve nutrient content claims such as trans fat-free or low trans fat due to the lack of a recommended daily value for trans fats. However, the agency planned a consumer study to evaluate public understanding of such claims and potentially consider regulations allowing their use on packaged foods. 12. The FDA defines trans fats as containing one or more trans double bonds that are not in a conjugated system, distinguishing synthetic non-conjugated trans fats from naturally occurring fatty acids with conjugated trans double bonds, such as conjugated linoleic acid. 13. Critics, including FDA advisors, argued that the 0.5 grams per serving threshold for labeling trans fat as 0 grams was too high, as individuals consuming multiple servings or products could still ingest significant amounts of trans fat. 14. Despite this, the FDA estimated that by 2009, trans fat labeling would prevent 600 to 1,200 cases of coronary heart disease and 250 to 500 deaths annually. This benefit was attributed to consumers choosing lower-trans-fat alternatives and manufacturers reducing trans fat content in their products. 15. Some U.S. cities have taken action to reduce trans fat consumption. 16. In May 2005, Tiburon, California, became the first U.S. city where all restaurants voluntarily used trans fat-free oils for cooking. 17. Montgomery County, Maryland, approved a ban on partially hydrogenated oils, becoming the first county in the nation to restrict trans fats. 18. New York City launched a campaign to reduce trans fat consumption, citing heart disease as the leading cause of death among residents. This included public education efforts and requests for restaurants to voluntarily eliminate trans fats from their menus. 19. After finding the voluntary program ineffective, New York City's Board of Health solicited public comments on a proposal to ban artificial trans fats in restaurants. On December 5, 2006, the board voted to implement the ban, making New York the first large U.S. city to strictly limit trans fats in restaurants. By July 1, 2007, restaurants were required to limit trans fats to 0.5 grams per serving, with full compliance across all foods by July 1, 2008. 20. Philadelphia also passed a trans fat ban, with the City Council voting unanimously on February 8, 2007, and the law signed by Mayor John F. Street on February 15, 2007. By September 1, 2007, eateries were required to stop frying food in trans fats, and by the following year, trans fats were prohibited as an ingredient in commercial kitchens. The law did not apply to prepackaged foods sold in the city. 21. On October 10, 2007, Philadelphia's City Council approved the use of trans fats by small bakeries throughout the city. 22. Albany County, New York, passed a trans fat ban following a unanimous vote by the county legislature on May 14, 2007. However, no implementation plan was established. 23. Legislators received a letter from Rick J. Sampson, president and CEO of the New York State Restaurant Association, urging them to delay action until the full impact of New York City's ban was understood. 24. Chicago considered a ban on oils containing trans fats for large chain restaurants. 25. On December 19, 2006, Massachusetts state representative Peter Koutoujian filed the first state-level legislation to ban restaurants from preparing foods with trans fats. 26. Similarly, Maryland, California, and Vermont considered statewide bans on trans fats. 27. King County, Washington, passed a ban on artificial trans fats, effective February 1, 2009. 28. The 2007 Indiana State Fair implemented a complete ban on trans fats in cooking oils used at the event. 29. The J.M. Smucker Company, the American manufacturer of Crisco, reformulated its products in 2004 to reduce trans fat content. The new formulation used solid saturated palm oil blended with soybean and sunflower oils, reducing trans fat content to less than 1 gram per serving. By January 24, 2007, all Crisco shortening products in the U.S. were reformulated to contain less than 1 gram of trans fat per serving while maintaining lower saturated fat content than butter. The separately marketed trans-fat-free version introduced in 2004 was discontinued. 30. On May 22, 2004, Unilever announced the elimination of trans fats from all its margarine products in Canada, including its flagship Becel brand. 31. Bunge Limited, through its Bunge Oils division, began producing and marketing a line of non-hydrogenated oils, margarines, and shortenings made from corn, canola, and soybean oils. 32. Some major food chains have voluntarily removed or reduced trans fats in their products. In other cases, legal actions targeting food vendors have prompted changes, often accompanied by significant media attention.
